Well, hon. gentlemen must know, and if they do not, certainly no member of this House knows better than the hon. leader of the Opposition himself,

that I should be giving incontestable evidence of my incompetency for my present post, that I should be showing once and for all that I had no sense of the responsibility of office, if I were, in a debate on the Address, to state what the duty on any article would be in the revision of the tariff. It would be interesting indeed if the right hon. leader of the Opposition-than whom no one knows better the duties of. a minister or of a Solicitor General, who is not a minister, in regard to anticipating the Budget Speech-would inform the House what "was in the back of his head when he said, 'Hear, hear,' in response to the request of the hon. member for Guysborough that I should announce the Government's position as to the duty on wheat and on agricultural implements. The time will come when both subjects will be fit subjects for discussion in this House. The revision of the tariff will be made in due course. When it is made, I, as associated with the Government, will do one of two things-I will accept full responsibility for the tariff as promulgated in that revision, or if I cannot do so I will sever my present association with the Government. When the tariff is revised, free wheat, agricultural implements and all other such matters will be fit and proper subjects for discussion. And I will be right in at the death; the hon. gentlemen's curiosity shall be satisfied to the limit.
I have heard considerable discussion of a topic on which I purpose specially to treat, a subject that now is first brought before the Canadian people and one which in its present form at all events has never yet before been the subject of discussion in this House-free food. Apparently many hon. gentlemen opposite see value in the free food cry. - On the other hand, judging from the vagaries of hon. gentlemen opposite, there is a very powerful section of their party who see very little value in free food as a political issue. There is little to be gained, perhaps, in discussing the merits of the question, because we are not sure yet where the Opposition stands with regard to it. We are not sure whether this policy of free food is to be inscribed upon their banner or not. It was put there on the 26th of November, 1913, hut it is notably absent from the amendment submitted in this debate by the leader of the Opposition. Therefore, in doubt as we are as to the adhesion of the Opposition to this cry, very little can be gained by extended discussion. But, as to those on both sides of the House who see at present in Canada .
nothing to be gained by the free food policy, those who would regret, and regret exceedingly, its	adoption as a	part of	the	tariffpolicy of	the Dominion,	I can	give	themthis consolation,-that there is little to fear in that regard. In the speech that the leader of the Opposition delivered in the city of Hamilton when he threw out the gospel of free food to the people,	he	tookcare to	warn them	that	he	was
a very cautious politician. He took care to tell them as regards his last cry, reciprocity, there was not much more to be said. He had no recriminations to make in regard to it, and the sentence with which he closed his reference to it was that it was his prayer that the dead past would bury its dead. He went on then to propound the new gospel of free food, but he added this very suggestive sentence, as quoted from his speech as reported in the Toronto 'Globe':
During the fifteen years that we were in office we had been very chary in making any alteration in the tariff. The reason is that when we place a tariff of customs duties we create an atmosphere in which our manufactures and industries are developed and if you were, to cut out or remove that tariff all of a sudden, the result would he very injurious.
Following out the principle of action that he there expounded, he admits that the Government retained virtually the National Policy with microscopic modifications, to use the very excellent vocabulary of the hon. member for Bed Deer (Mr Clark); and the reason he did not put his changes into force sooner was that it would be too sudden and that it would cause a shock to the commercial mechanism of Canada. So to those who feel in their hearts that free trade, if it became a matter of practice instead of a matter of preaching and theory in Canada, would be something to be feared, for them there is this word of consolation, that the right hon. the leader of the Opposition has all the years to think about it between now and the time when he gets into office, and many may he the .variations that he may decide upon in that time; and then, after he gets in, he will have fifteen years for deliberation, because if he Should enforce it and so radically modify the tariff all of a sudden, it would mean disaster to the industries of Canada. So. at all events for this generation now living, we have little to fear from the new doctrine of free food.
What I purpose to deal with most is the question of the Highways Bill. It has been alluded to, I believe by all, or almost all of the hon. gentlemen opposite who have taken part in this debate, and a vigorous attempt

has been made to throw the onus of the rejection of that Bill upon the Government of the day. It has been said by the hon. member for Red Deer, and repeated or echoed by the hon. member for North Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) and the hon. member for Guvs-borough (Mr. Sinclair) that all of the unfavourable impression that was made upon the country by its rejection by the Senate was entirely dissipated since they had an opportunity of thoroughly explaining it to the people. I wondered, as they talked, what explanation they gave the people. I wondered if they gave the innocent people the explanation they ventured to give this House. Was not the House struck by the careful study apparently that had been made of this Bill by the hon. member for Guysborough, who stood in his place and stated that five clauses of the Bill had been passed by the Senate and that because they rejected the last clause was no reason for blaming them for rejecting the Bill, or the statement made by the hon. member for Red Deer, usually a little more careful, that five clauses of the Bill had been passed by the Senate and only the sixth clause had been touched when, as a matter of fact, everybody knows that five clauses were never passed by the Senate either in 1912 or in 1913 and that the sixth clause was never passed at all, that the fourth clause was amended in both years and the sixth rejected in both years. The question before the House is whether or not this Government were justified in rejecting the altered Bill as it was brought down by the Senate or whether they should have accepted it. If this Government should have accepted it, all things considered, the onus is on this Government. If they should not have accepted it the onus is on the Senate and to that point I purpose directing my discussion.	,
What was the Highways Bill? The Highways Bill, as brought down in both years in the same form each time, was a Bill containing five clauses the effect of all of which was to empower the Government of the day to expend such money as might be voted in the Supply Bill through the agencies of the provincial governments upon a comprehensive system of highway improvement. The preamble of the Bill set out that it was desirable in Canada to enter upon a comprehensive and useful system of improvement of the highways in order that the general transportation facilities of the country might be made what they ought to be. The Bill then went on to say that the Government might divide among the provincial
governments, upon such terms as might be mutually agreed upon between the two governments, a sum of money to be voted in the ordinary way in the Supply Bill.
It further stated in clause six that in addition to that power the Government of the day should have the right, with the consent both of the legislature and of the Lieutenant Governor in Council of the province in question, to expend the money directly upon highways if they conceived such was the better course. That is to say, that such share or part of such share as might afterwards be voted in the Supply Bill to a province might, with the consent and approval of the Government of that province and of the legislature as well, be expended through the direct agency of this Government upon this general scheme of highway improvement. That was the sum and substance of the Bill. It was sought to be amended in this House. It was stated by hon. gentlemen opposite and argued most vigorously that a clause should be inserted binding the Government to divide that money proportionately between the provinces and further stated that clause six should be eliminated and whether or not both the provincial and the Dominion governments conceived it to be in the interests of the country that the money should be expended through the direct agency of this Government, they should be stripped of power to do so. These two were the contentions advanced by hon. gentlemen opposite. I would be the last to argue that this House should not have the say now and at all times as to the distribution of this money, as to the principle of its distribution and I should likewise be the last to argue that the general principle of that distribution should not be on the basis of population, proportionate to the population of each province. I propose to argue first of all that the Government was not only justified but was bound to reject the Senate amendment on the ground that these amendments were not in the interests of the Bill and, were vitally antagonistic to the principle and purpose of the Bill and I shall argue that, aside entirely from the merits of the amendments a greater principle was in question, that of the power of the Senate to interfere by amendment in such a Bill and that, aside from the merits altogether, this Government would not have been justified; would have been truant to its trust and to the people of this country, had they accepted these amendments. Now, on the first point, 1 have acceded that this House must always maintain as part of its prerogative and part

of its duty the control of expenditures and its division among the provinces and that furthermore the general principle of that division should be under ordinary circumstances, a principle of proportion to the population of each province. Then why reject the amendment to clause four proposed by hon. gentlemen opposite, which provided that the Government should be disabled from expending that money in any other method than by the hard and fast rule of expenditure in proportion to population. It must be remembered, first of all, and I cannot impress this too strongly upon hon. gentlemen here, that the Bill known as the Highways Bill did not set aside any specific sum of money from the treasury of Canada. It simply provided machinery by which, when the money was set aside or voted by this House, it should be used through the agencies of the provincial governments for the benefits of our common highways. That was the purpose and end of the Bill. It was essential because ordinarily the control of highways is not within the jurisdiction of this Parliament under the British North America Act, and if we chose to use the agencies of provincial governments, the Bill was essential that we might do so. This House might have undoubtedly, by simply declaring the improvement of this highway or that highway was necessary for the general advantage of Canada, (with the sanction of Parliament), expended the money when and where it liked without the agency of any Bill at all; but in order to secure the benefit of the machinery of the provincial governments and to avoid duplication and the frittering away of money on worthless machinery, the Government decided to put through a Bill to utilize the machinery already provided. Having shown that no money was specifically appropriated or set aside out of the treasury of Canada by that Bill, it will be apparent to all that the Bill did not require to be first of all premised by an introductory resolution, that it did not need to be anticipated by the sanction of the Governor General himself. By section 54 of the British North America Act that is essential in one circumstance and one only, that is when the Bill itself sets aside a specific amount of money for a specific purpose. When that is done, the sanction of the Governor General must be secured. That was not done by this Bill, but none the less the Bill, ordinarily speaking, was a money Bill, in that it designated the purpose for which money afterwards voted should be spent.
It will be seen, therefore, that for the rea-.
son, and the very clear reason, that no money was voted by the Bill, a subsequent Bill would be necessary in order to vote the money, and that subsequent Bill would have to be introduced by resolution sanctioned by the Governor General of Canada; and in that subsequent Bill it would have to be provided how and on what principle the money should be distributed through the provinces. Now, it will be clear to the hon. member for Red Deer that the House of Commons of Canada, in refusing to specify in advance in the enabling Bill- the Highways Bill-that this money should for all time be distributed pro rata according to population, did not in any way alienate from itself the right to say that that should be the basis of distribution. This House still had the right to say in the Supply Bill which was to follow, and which alone was to vote the money, how that money should be divided, and upon what principle it should be distributed, and this House not only had the right, but was bound to say so in that Supply Bill which was to follow. Why then was it necessary, why then was it of value that the clause should be inserted in the Highway Bill itself ? By what right do hon. gentlemen opposite argue that this House in the year 1913 or 1914 should bind the hands of the Commons for years and years to come in regard to the distribution of this money? So long as the right and the power is vested in this House to determine the distribution, then this House has reserved to itself every right it has or ought to have, and that right was reserved and was reserved to be exercised in the way it always has been and always should be exercised. Does anybody deny that?
In the light of the explanation which the hon. gentleman has given, what is the use of the sixth clause?

I am coming to the sixth clause and I am not at all surprised that the hon. gentleman should desire to get past his argument on the fourth clause. This House had the power and always has had the power to decide as to the distribution of the money of the people of Canada and this House never can, at all events never should, divest itself of that right and power. I ask again what right is there in the Commons of Canada of 1913 to tie the hands of the Commons of Canada of 1917 as to the method of distribution? Is it not the Commons of that day that should decide as to how the money of that day should be

divided? Does my hon. friend from Eed Deer think that a superior wisdom is resident in the members of this House to-day over what is likely to reside in them five years from now? Why should we abbreviate now the power that we claim to be so valuable for the Commons of years to come? So that not only was no good object to be served but a very bad object would have been served and a bad principle would have been adopted if we had attempted to put in a general Bill that hard and fast restriction. I have admitted that ordinarily the principle of distribution should he that of pro rata according to population. Is that disputed by any one in this House ? But does any hon. gentleman say that circumstances might not arise when he himself would vote for a different principle of distribution ? Does any hon. gentleman say that he cannot imagine those circumstances? If so, then why does he vote to tie the hands of Parliament in this regard ? Nobody rises to say he cannot imagine such circumstances. Why ? Because every hon. gentleman opposite voted for a different system of distribution in a very similar Bill. That is why they do not rise. The hon. member for Guysborough says:-

You are not
teaching school to-night.
The hon. member says we are not teaching school. It might be of advantage to him if some one would.
That is very, very smart.

I say they know they have voted for a different principle of distribution and they voted for it in the same session. I may inform, though I am not teaching school, the hon. member for Guysborough that the principle of distribution according to population was not followed in the agricultural instruction Bill at all. A different principle was followed approximating to it, but not that principle itself. In the Agricultural Instruction Bill the principle was to distribute the first $20,000 of money to the provinces, and there was also to be distributed a certain fixed sum -$20,000 I think it was-to veterinary colleges-two inroads upon the principle of proportionate distribution; and all the hon. gentlemen opposite voted and voted without question for that distribution. Why then should they tie the hands of future parliaments from adopting a principle which they themselves have already adopted in the
distribution of money? There are circumstances that one might easily imagine when it would not only be not the best but would be positively bad legislation to distribute the money according to population. In the year 1913 no such circumstances existed, and the Supply Bill, which was brought down as evidence of the good faith of the Government, did vote the money and did divide it on a population basis. But if that Were followed as an inexorable law, if it were known to the various provinces that it was going'to be followed, come what may, then it would be quite within the power of the province to say: ' We are going to get our money from the Dominion Government for highway improvements and we will restrict our own expenditure on highway improvements and let the Dominion Government do it. The result would he that, instead of this policy resulting in the improvement of the highways, it would simply result in the money being spent in some other way by the provinces and Canada paying for the highways of the provinces instead of the provinces themselves. I do not think that the hon. member for Carleton, N.B. (Mr. Carvell) will compliment me by saying that that is a very great stretch of imagination or of ingenuity. I thfnk it will be plain to him that it is not only a possible but a quite probable result.

As far as I know,
the several provinces in Canada will want to spend all the money they can get from this Government, or all the money thev can get from any other source whatever, in order to make the highways what they ought to be. But my hon. friend is drawing on his imagination to the full extent if he thinks that if the Dominion Government and Parliament pay the money, and if they trust these provinces, they will refuse to do their proper share in connection with the improvements of the highways.

I have no doubt that they will be willing to spend what money they can get, but they might save their own money for other purposes. That being the case it will be seen that there would have been no object at all, and that a very bad principle would have been imbedded in our methods, if we had adopted the suggestion of hon. gentlemen opposite and put this hard and fast rule into the Bill. We reserve for this House of Commons all its powers and rights in this regard, we strip it of no part of its prerogative at all. We held for 1913. rnd all the years there are to follow, the right

to determine once and for all how the highway money was to be spent.
Now, for fear I might forget it, the hon. member for Guysborough referred to an amendment which he mentioned, but which he did not read, by the hon. member for Carleton to the effect that the Senate having stripped the Bill of clause 6 and having so amended clause 4 by this cumbersome method, we should have accepted the Bill, or that the Bill being dropped, we should simply have come forward in our Supply Bill and voted money into the treasuries of the provinces. I ask what power would have been retained by this Government to see that the money so voted into the provincial treasuries was expended for the purpose for which it was voted? No conditions could have been attached to the Supply Bill. The conditions in the Highway Bill were swept away. The money would have been simply spilled into the treasuries of the provinces and the provinces would have been depended upon to spend the money for highways. Is that fulfilling our duties as the Government of Canada? The hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) will not say so, I know. The hon. member for Edmonton will not stand up in his place in this debate and say that this Government is relieved of its obligations to the people by voting money into the provincial treasuries.
We know that there is a part
9 p.m. of the moneys of the Dominion
Government in respect to which we do relieve ourselves of all obligations of trusteeship by voting it into the provincial treasuries and that part is represented by the annual subsidies because that is a part of the framework of our constitution. But the words of the constitution apply to no other moneys whatever. As for all other moneys that are not so designated by the British North America Act and amending Acts we are the trustees, we can never divest ourselves of that responsibility, and we have no right whatever to vote that money into the treasuries of the provinces and not to follow it and see that it reaches its proper destination. We must, if we are true to our trust as guardians and custodians of the money of the people, see that the money gets to its ultimate destination and see that it is spent for the purpose for which it is intended and we must trust to the responsibility of no other Government but our own in that regard.
If I were to quote an authority in opposition to the contention of the hon. member for Guysborough, I would quote the hon.
.
member for Edmonton himself, because he said in his place in the House just last session, and argued at some length, with great force and with correctness, that this Government would not be justified in so voting money into the treasuries of the provinces but that this Government was bound to follow this money and see that the money was spent for the purpose for which it was intended.
My hon. friend has been good enough to mention my name and to ask for my opinion.
No, I have stated the opinion the hon. gentleman has given.
I would like to say that my hon. friend has not stated the opinion I gave in regard to the Highways Bill.

I have quoted the hon. gentleman, and quoted him with approval, on the question of the responsibility of Parliament for the money entrusted to us and as to whether we can relieve ourselves of out trust by voting money into the provincial treasuries as suggested by the hon. member for Guysborough. I have quoted him against the contention of the hon. member for Guysborough, and I have *quoted him with absolute correctness.

May I
ask the hon. gentleman a question? I followed his argument very closely. What objection is there to increasing the subsidies of the provinces in order to help the provinces to get better roads?

I am afraid my hon.
friend has not followed me very closely.
Yes, I have.

Because I have stated that if it were done by the methods advised by the hon. member for Guysborough there would be no machinery and no method by which this Government could see that the money was spent to the best advantage of the people and that it was spent for the purpose for which it was intended. The responsibility to see to that would be shifted from the shoulders of the Government to the shoulders of the several provinces and we have no right to so divest ourselves of our responsibilities.
Might you not do that by amending the British North America Act?
Perhaps so, but that is not the suggestion of the hon. member for Guysborough.

No, but on general
principles.

The British North
America Act is not amended yet, but the hon. member for Guysborougli homes forward and says we ought to do it without an amendment and that we are truant to our principles because we do not.
Under what authority has the constitution and practice of the Dominion of Canada placed the roads up to date?

I stated that in the
early part of my address but I will repeat it more fully if the hon. member desires it; that is, I will give my own opinion for what it is worth. The highways of Canada are within the jurisdiction of the provincial legislatures, in so far as they are local. At the same time, the Dominion Parliament would have jurisdiction over a highway that had become of a national character say by reason of its passing from one province to another and we could exercise our jurisdiction over any highway if we adopted the method so often utilized of declaring that the improvements, or any special works upon a highway, were for the general advantage of Canada. But by reason of the general principle that highways are within the provincial jurisdiction, then, in order to enable us properly to act and at the same time properly to conserve the rights of the Canadian people and discharge our own duties to the full, we require an Act by which the machinery of the provinces may be used for the purpose of spending this money, but all the same, we are able, by virtue of the conditions imposed and plans devised and accepted, to follow that money to its destination in order to see that it is spent on a general, and uniform and useful system and that it does the greatest good to the greatest number of our people.

Would the hon. gentleman be good enough to state to the House what he considers to be the reason why the provincial governments cannot fully and properly be trusted with the expenditure of any money that is necessary and available for the improvement of the highways?
That is not the question at all. Whether they can be trusted or whether they cannot be trusted we have no right to lay upon them a responsibility that the constitution fixes upon us.

I understand my hon.
friend to admit that the constitution places the responsibility regarding roads upon the provinces and not upon the Dominion.

Very well, but so far
as the expenditure of the money of the Canadian people in the Dominion treasury is concerned, be that expenditure upon highways or upon anything else, that trusteeship is vested here, and the hon. member for Edmonton is himself a most vociferous authority that we can never strip ourselves of that responsibility.

I see a very vast difference between expenditure by this Government on purposes for which this Parliament is responsible, and expenditure on purposes for which the provincial governments and legislatures are responsible.
Does the hon. gentleman believe that expenditure for educational purposes differs constitutionally speaking from expenditure for highway purposes?
I certainly do.
Then the hon. gentleman must be informed and informed very quickly that education also is within the jurisdiction of the provincial legislatures.
I do not know that it is exclusively within the jurisdiction of the provincial legislatures, or otherwise, this Parliament has gone out of its way to vote money for technical education.

And we have voted
money for highways, and education is just as exclusively within provincial jurisdiction as the highways are within provincial jurisdiction.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I will ask the House to keep in mind that the discussion so far has entirely centered upon the merits of the amendments themselves. The argument, so' far as I have been able to advance it, is, that on the merits, the amendment to clause 6 should have been rejected and must have been rejected by any government that remembered its duty to the Canadian people. As to clause 6: It will be recalled that the Senate not only amended clause 4 by fastening upon it this hard and fast system of distribution, but also entirely struck out clause 6 which provided:
The minister, with the approval of the Governor in Council and upon such terms and conditions as are prescribed by order in council, may undertake the construction of any high-

way or the improvement of any highway in any existing province and may expend in such improvement or construction the whole or any part of the sums voted by Parliament for such subsidy to that province.
Provided, further, that the minister shall first obtain the necessary authority from the legislature of such province and the consent of the Lieutenant-Governor in Council.
That is to say, if, as a result of the joint wisdom of the Government of Canada and of the legislature and government of the province with which we may be dealing for the time being, it is decided that better results could be obtained by expending the money through the direct machinery of this Government, this Government should have the power to do so. It must be remembered that before that could be done provision must be made by the legislature of the province in question as well as the consent of the Lieutenant-Governor in Council of that province obtained before the Government of Canada itself could exercise that right. That clause was reviewed in very alarming terms by the hon. member for Eed Deer; he said it was meant to catch votes, and he proclaimed that it should never be allowed in this country, that this Government should be able to go and spend money here and there, because if they had that right they could make promises and catch votes. But his concern for the result of this clause was tame even, compared with the concern of the leader of the majority in the Senate. In order that the full import of this may be clear to the House, the name of the leader of the majority in the Senate should be mentioned, Sir George Ross, ex-Prime Minister of the province of Ontario. He feared the pressure that we would be able to exercise over the legislature; he said we would be able to put our hands upon the legislature and say, 'Do as we say or we will not give you money, and the legislature in terror would submit. And that pressure, the leader of the Senate held to be a very great invasion of the constitutional rights of Canada. He said:
That means that the Dominion Government is putting its hand upon the legislature of a whole province to swing that legislature to its own ends.
Hear, hear

Now did you ever hear of anything of greater enormity than that? Suppose the Imperial Government put its hand upon the whole representation of Scotland, or on the one hundred and three members for Ireland, by some financial consideration, in order to swing them around to some policy of the government. I believe Lord Castlereagh did that in 1800. Ireland
,
was brought into the union with England and Scotland.

And he committed suicide afterwards.
So that the vocabulary of the hon. member for Red Deer is quite outdone by the vividly expressed fears of the leader of the majority in the Senate. He describes the Highways Bill as the greatest enormity he thinks he ever heard perpetrated since one hundred and thirteen years ago when, he says, Ireland was brought into the Union by a wholesale system of oppression and constraint.
One would think in the first place that hon. gentlemen opposite had never heard of any such pressure having been brought to bear before; that they never heard of the insertion in any Bill of a clause such as this. And it may be a matter of surprise to the hon. member for Guysborough-because I do not think he has spent a very great deal of time considering this subject-it ;may be a matter of surprise to him to be told that he himself and the other side of the House in general allowed to go through this House, without a division and I believe without debate, a clause on exactly the same lines in another Bill of similar purport. I refer to the Agricultural Instruction Bill of 1913. The Agricultural Instruction Bill of 1913 set by a specific sum of money, $10,000,000; $700,000 for 1913; $800,000 for the following year, and so on, until $10,000,000 should be appropriated for the purpose of agricultural education. The Bill went on to provide means by which this money should be spent through the agencies of the provincial governments along a system to be outlined by this Dominion Government, and by which the machinery of the provincial governments should be utilized for the purpose of the expenditure of this money and of getting the greatest results therefrom. And the Bill went on to provide a clause similar in terms, though not exact in terms,-and I shall point out the difference later,-it went on to provide a clause similar in terms to clause 6 of the Highways Bill, and that clause was passed by this House with the assent of hon. gentlemen opposite, and it passed the Senate as well. The Agricultural Instruction Bill, clause 7, voted money for education in agriculture in these terms:
The Governor in Council may make such regulations as are deemed advisable for giving effect to the object and purpose of this Act. And notwithstanding anything in this Act, the minister with the approval of the Governor in Council and with the consent of the Lieutenant-Governor in Council of any province_

Hon. members opposite will remember that that is all the consent that has to be obtained.
-and upon such terms and conditions as are prescribed by the Governor in Council, may expend in any such province in any year the whole or any part of the grant provided by the province under this Act for the purpose set forth in the preamble to this Act.
If any hon. gentleman opposite can explain upon what principle he votes for that clause of the Agricultural Bill and denies his vote for a similar clause in the Highways Bill, I would like to hear that explanation. The only difference between the two clauses is this, that whereas in the Highways Bill this Government, in order to expend the money directly on agricultural education, must first obtain the consent not only of the Government of the province but of the Legislature as well; on the contrary, in the Agricultural Instruction Bill, this Government may spend the money directly without the agency of the province, but only upon the consent of the Government, and not of the Legislature at all. This Bill was voted upon and put through, after the similar clause in the Highways Bill was denied in 1912 by hon. gentlemen opposite and by the Senate at their dictation. So the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark) should have explained upon what principle he believes this clause 7 not only innocuous but valuable and denies to the Government clause 6 of the Highways Bill. Why should clause 6 be in? Can hon. members opposite not conceive of circumstances under which it would be advisable and expeditious and economical to spend the money directly under the Dominion Government, in a special case, rauier than through the agency of a provincial government? Presuming, for example, that it is a road that runs between the provinces, presuming tlfat the machinery for improvement is more convenient, would it not be advisable so to spend the money without utilizing the machinery of the two provinces? The spirit of the Bill was to utilize the two provinces, but it was only right and proper that means should be provided in special cases, and if both parties should consider it advisable, the money should be spent directly. In the case of money voted for agricultural instruction it might be U3ed, and the power might be used if a government saw fit in order to invite votes in special localities. They might go to a special locality and say: Here, we will establish an agricultural college here; we will establish an experimental station.
Not nearly so handy as roads.

If the hon. member
came from the province of Saskatchewan I could understand his familiarity with the use of such clauses in respect of roads. At all events the hon. member's mind must admit that the principle is exactly the same; and if there is vice in one there i3 vice in the other; and that if he votes against one, to be at all consistent, he must vote against the other, but he did not do it. Now, I have pointed out that circumstances might easily be foreseen, under which it would be advisable and in the interests of Canada that the money should be expended directly under the agency of the Government of Canada. Consequently no purpose could possibly be served by the elimination of clause six. Why? If we are to act on the fears of hon. gentlemen opposite; if that principle is to govern our legislation in this House, what are we going to pass? We shall have to repeal the Public Works Act. The Public Works Act provides that the Government of this country, through the Public Works Department may spend money here, there and anywhere thorough-out the country, and presumably that money can be used for political purposes. If the principle is right that that power should be denied the Government, then I say we should repeal the main provisions of the Public Works Act. If this power should be denied the Dominion Government, it should be denied the provincial governments; it should be denied to all governments. Then I ask:	How are we
going to have our institutions built or controlled at all? We have to entrust such power to our governments but a principle of our constitution is that our governments are held directly responsible for the use of that power, and we would not protect the people by abridging their power. We protect the people by holding the Government alone accountable for the exercise of the power reposed in them. The Government has never in any way endeavoured to evade that responsibility, and I trust it never will. So much for the merits of the two amendments as they stand themselves.
I come now to a more powerful objection, an objection that to my mind appears insuperable, and that I venture to think will appear utterly insuperable to hon. gentlemen opposite if they will only give their minds fair play. I make the argument, that I now propose to make, with special con-

fidence to the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark), because I believe that if he fully apprehended the significance of the Senate's action in this regard, he would be the last to approve of their interference. The hon. member for Red Deer apparently has not read in the records of the Commons both of 1912 and 1913 the real reasons placed upon ' Hansard ' for the rejection of the Senate's amendments. I have not heard them quoted, I have scarcely heard the main reasons referred to by hon. gentlemen opposite, and I am at a loss to understand the educating influences of those speeches that have been delivered by which they have switched the population of this country against the Government of the day and behind the matured wisdom of the Senate, because they have utterly ignored the main reasons stated by the Government for the rejection of the Senate's amendments. It is a matter which should be, at least in general terms, within the knowledge of all that the Senate of this country has no power either to initiate or to amend or to interfere with Bills appropriating money; nor have they power in any way, by methods direct or by methods indirect, to circumvent or in any way at all to affect the distribution of the public money. That is a principle of the constitution, not only of this country, but of the mother country, from which we derived it. It is not a new one; it has been in force there with growing strength since 1628. It has been affirmed and reaffirmed time without number, and violated in any important instance, yes in any material instance, never since that time. It is true the Lords of England, who are in a position analogous to the Senate of Canada, have ventured in certain instances to interfere with such Bills by methods sometimes indirect, sometimes direct, to affect the expenditure of money, to affect the conditions under which it should be expended; but they have done it by a direct negative of the Bill in question, and it is generally argued, and, I believe, generally accepted, that the Lords and the Senate of this country, while they have not the power to amend or interfere in that way, have the power of rejection. But I can point out even this in that regard, that the Prime Minister of Great Britain on the 2nd of December, 1909, argued with very great force, if not with resistless force, that the power of rejection as well as the power of amendment was dormant, moribund and for all practical purposes dead. It may be questioned even now if the power of rejection is as intact as it was years ago;
[Mr. Meighenl.	#
and as to the power iof the Lords in England or the Senate in Canada, it is generally accepted that, whether by methods direct or by methods indirect, they are without power to interfere by amendment and if they have the power to interfere at all they must take the full responsibility of rejection. I do not think that I shall be asked by hon. gentlemen in this House to support what I have said by quotation. Back, as far as 1628, the Commons of England, on the advice of the law Lords, tomitted from all such Bills reference to the Lords and made such Bills the Acts of the Commons alone. And in 1771, by a standing order of the House, the following was reaffirmed as the law of England:
That all aids and supplies granted to His Majesty by Parliament are the sole gift of the Commons, and all Bills for granting such aids and supplies ought to begin with the Commons, as it is the undoubted and sole right of the Commons to direct, limit and appoint any and all such Bills, the ends, purposes, considerations, conditions, limitations and qualifications of such grants, which ought not to be changed or altered by the House of Lords.
This is as far back as 1671, or, to make it more easy to remember for the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark), about one hundred years before Adam Smith was born, at all events before he wrote his ' Wealth of Nations.'

Will the hon. gentleman permit me to correct him? Adam Smith published his ' Wealth of Nations ' in 1776, and so the hon. gentleman has proven that Adam Smith wrote his book two years before he was born.

I said, at all events
before he wrote the ' Wealth of Nations.' I did not pretend to be exact, but I think I may pay myself a compliment, because, though I had not looked up the date, I guessed it within two years. It is the law of England as set forth in the words I have quoted that taxes and the appropriation of taxes, are the sole prerogative of the Commons and that the consent of the Crown and of the peers is necessary only to clothe it with the form of law. We in this country, by a standing order passed in 1873, reaffirmed the same as the prerogative of the Commons of Canada and as entirely beyond the jurisdiction of the Senate of Canada. That will be found in the Rules of this House, and, so far as I recollect, the rule is word for word with the standing order of the British House of 1671. So, not only have the

Senate no power to initiate, but they have no power to ' direct, limit or appoint ' the ' ends, purposes, considerations, conditions, limitations and qualifications ' of such grants. These are the words, taken from the standing orders of this House, always affirmed to be the law of Canada, and until this Bill was put through, never materially invaded by the Senate iof Canada. Now, it may be said that inasmuch as this Bill does not specifically appropriate money from the treasury, it is not a money Bill, and the Senate therefore has a right to interfere. It is not a money Bill in the sense that it does not appropriate specific money, but it is a money Bill in that it directs, limits, makes conditions and qualifications under which money afterwards to be voted is to be expended; and the Senate of Canada have no power under the constitution in anv way to limit or affect the qualifications under which money to be voted shall be expended. So, it is a money Bill so far as the power of the Senate to amend it is concerned. What purpose could it serve to say that they have no power to interfere with the provision of a Supply Bill and alter the purposes to which money voted in the Supply Bill shall be directed, if they have power, in the case of this Bill, to make alterations and in that way divert money to be voted under a Supply Bill? It is only a roundabout way of getting at the same thing; they are interfering with the conditions and qualifications of the appropriation of the money of the people of Canada voted by the people's representatives. It is clear that for three hundred years this has been beyond the prerogative of the Lords, and it has always been beyond the prerogative of the Senate of Canada. It would be an anomaly, an absurdity, if this House were to quietly accept amendments so made by the Senate in derogation of our rights, no matter what may be the merits of the proposed change. The greater principle is superimposed, for it is the duty, and one of the first duties of the Commons of Canada, representing the people of this country, to preserve to ourselves the prerogative that has been ours for generations, and that has been the protection of the British people for centuries, and not meekly to abrogate our powers in favour of any irresponsible body, or of any body whatever. That is the great duty imposed upon us, a duty from which this Government will not shrink. We are the custodians of that right, and we do not propose to have it robbed from us bv anv body of men. What would be the result, it II
we meekly sat down under this Senate amendment?

I did not follow the
hon. gentleman's arguments very closely. As a matter of the history of this Bill, will he please tell me whether it was dealt with as a money Bill when it was introduced in this House?

I have already dealt
fully with that. When the Bill was brought forward for the second reading, the right hon. leader of the Opposition objected on the ground that there had been no recommendation or sanction of the Bill bv His Royal Highness the Governor General, and that the Bill had not been introduced bv resolution, and the right hon. gentleman argued that it was a money Bill. The leader of the Government objected, not that it was not a money Bill, but that it did not appropriate specific money and therefore did not come under the rule which requires the preliminary sanction of the Governor General. The Bills that reauire to be so introduced are Bills appropriating part of the public revenue for a specific purpose, which this Bill did not do. Now. that must be clear. Whether the hon. member for North Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie) calls that a ' money bill ' does not matter.
Then it was not dealt with as a money Bill in this House?

' Money bill ' is only a name. This Bill did not appropriate any specific part of the public revenue, and for that reason it did not require to he introduced by resolution. The hon. member can call it a money Bill, or a silver Bill, or anything else he pleases. It did not possess that element of a money Bill, but it did possess another element. Let me get this into the mind of the hon. member for North Cape Breton, and then I am sure that every other member of this House will understand it clearly. I say it did possess another characteristic of a money Bill, as it proposed a purpose to which money afterwards to be appropriated should be put. It provided the conditions and qualifications under which money afterwards to be voted should be spent. That is a characteristic and element of the Bill, and the Senate cannot interfere with that Bill because if they do it they are running contrary to the standing order of 1678, one of the elemental principles of our Constitution. Surely that must be clear. The hon. member from North Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie)-



perhaps I do not do justice to his mind, it may be that he refuses to have this made clear to his mind. He is trying to follow the example of his elder brothers in the Senate and he is endeavouring to shelter himself behind the phrase ' a money Bill,' which has one of two characteristics, if it is to provide money it must be preceded by a resolution and if, secondly, it is to provide the manner and the limitations under which it is to be expended it comes under the second classification and in either case the Senate cannot interfere.

I am learning fast. Does my hon. friend say that the authorities of this House made a mistake in allowing the Bill to go through without being preceded by a resolution or did they gloss it over and allow it to go through as a money Bill when it really is not a money Bill.

I have not the slightest question to make of the rectitude of the Speaker's decision when he decided that this Bill was not such a Bill as required a resolution, that it did not come within the clause of the rules of this House that describes when and under what conditions a Bill must be so introduced.
Do I understand my hon. friend to say that it underwent a process of evolution in going to the other House and became a money Bill?

Perhaps I can address myself with confidence to the task of overcoming the clouds in the brain of my hon. friend, but I cannot, with confidence, address myself to the task of overcoming his prejudices. It went through no evolution between here and the Senate, it was the same Bill there as here, he can call it a money Bill or anything he likes; it is not a Bill that came within the clause of our rules, a special clause providing for the introduction by resolution of a money Bill; but it was a Bill that, as plainly as the nose on his face, came within the rules that prevented it being interfered with by the Senate. The hon. gentleman will perhaps admit that it is not the same clause at all that describes a Bill so to be introduced and the clause that describes such a Bill as is without the pale of the Senate of Canada. They are altogether different, and the hon. member does not deceive anybody, I do not think he even deceives himself by harping on the expression ' money bill.'
That is unkind, the *word ' harping ' is not a nice one.

I invite my hon. friend to
get away from the phrase 'a money bill.' The Senate appeared to think that no Bill should be allowed to pass through appropriating money to the provinces, unless they themselves see to it that the money is properly distributed. In the first place, they have no right so to interfere. What right have they -to tie the hands of this House? What right have they to attempt to tie the hands of future Houses of Commons? If they can do this what is the position? After we have passed the Highways Bill we come to the Supply Bill, we go to vote this money to be spent under the provisions and subject to the qualifications set out in the Highways Bill. We have accepted the Senate amendment. We have allowed the Senate to dictate to this House how such money shall be distributed. We have allowed them to invade our prerogative to that extent. Then when the Highways Bill is under debate some hon. gentleman proposes: let us distribute this money according to the method followed in the Agricultural Instruction Act, let us divide so much money among all the provinces and let us distribute the rest according to population. Oh, some gentleman gets up and says, no, we cannot do that, we are forbidden to do that by the Senate amendment to the Highways Act. The hands of this House are tied by an amendment in the matter of the distribution of our money. Is such a course not an interference with the prerogative of this House to guide solely the distribution of our funds and the purposes to which the money of this country is to be put? The Senate has completely desecrated and has lifted entirely out of the Constitution the sole control of this House over the money of this country, if we permit the Senate to interpose as they proposed to interpose in the Highways Bill.
As I said before, one would imagine that it had been an immemorial principle of the Upper House never to permit a Bill of this kind to go through, appropriating money to provinces, unless it first of all dictated to this House the principle on which it was to be distributed. It will be a matter of surprise perhaps to hon. gentlemen opposite that just one year before the Senate fastened on this notion of inserting this amendment to clause 4, they allowed a similar Bill to go through with very little criticism and only twelve votes against it, which permitted money to be distributed among the provinces and did not stipulate any principle on which it was to be distributed, that was the [DOT] Agricultural Aid Bill of 1912. That bill provided in very terms that the Government of

Canada might give the various provinces sums to be voted afterwards in the Supply Bill to be used to aid agriculture and no clause was inserted in the Senate tying the hands of this House or of future Houses in the distribution of such money. Consequently the Senate itseilf is on record as acceding to the principle that this House and this House alone has the control of the distribution of money, whether that distribution is effected by one Bill or by two.
Furthermore, it was argued in the Senate of Canada that the whole Bill was unconstitutional, that inasmuch as highways were within the jurisdiction of the provinces we had no power to interfere at all, whether we employed the agencies of the provincial Government or not, that the whole Bill was in direct conflict with the constitution of Canada; and the leader of the Senate majority argued for that principle and argued lengthily if not strongly. But he did not take the responsibility of negativing the Bill. The Senate had the power if it had any power to interfere at all, to reject the Bill. If the Bill was unconstitutional or if he so believed, it was his duty, if he had the courage of his convictions, to negative the Highways Bill altogether. Why did he not do it? Why did he not ask his followers to give a direct negative to that Bill, and not ask them to take the roundabout method, which is only an excuse, of making the Bill impossible legislation by encumbering it with vicious amendments? The reason is apparent to every member in this House. The leader of the Liberal party in that House knew that no matter for what excuse he negatived that Bill it would be clear to the humblest intelligence in Canada that they had killed the Bill and he preferred to do it by a more ingenious method, by attaching to it amendments which he knew could not be accepted by this House or any other that had in its conscience the duty of preserving the prerogative of the people's representatives. He took the roundabout and indirect method rather of fastening an amendment to clause four and eliminating clause six, knowing, as he must have known, that by doing that they were accomplishing their aim perhaps in a manner that would provide an excuse, plausible to those who did not fully understand the question; but he refused to go about it in the direct and manly way of negativing the Bill as was in his power. So it resolves itself into this, that the Senate fastened on the Bill amendments that they knew were not in their power to pass, they knew that in lli
doing so they were flying in the face of one of the elemental principles of our constitution, they knew in doing it that no Government could possibly accept such an amendment, and they knew that the result would be to destroy the Highways Bill once and for all. Consequently it must be clear to anyone who does justice to his intelligence that their purpose from the beginning was to destroy the Highways Bill just as the result was to destroy the Highways Bill. There the responsibility lies. They took that responsibility knowing full well the result, and the responsibility being there we intend it shall remain there; and we do not propose that in the Highways Bill or in any other Bill the rights that have been the rights of the people's representatives throughout the history of this country and the mother country shall be invaded in any degree by the Senate of this country. If they attempt to invade those rights whatever may be their purpose, whether manfully stated or whether concealed, we propose to resist that usurpation and to maintain for ourselves the control over the expenditure, the control over the conditions, limitations, and qualifications of expenditure, which has been implanted in our Constitution and which has been there for many years gone by. For these reasons I say it must be clear to all that this House was not only well advised but this House was bound not only on the merits of the two amendments themselves but for a higher reason, for the reason that these amendments were brought down in violation of a principle of the Constitution which it is our duty to preserve-this House was bound I say for these two reasons to reject those amendments. It must be clear the Senate knew this House was so bound and the responsibility then is plain to all, and I believe it is plain to the hon. member for Red Deer. The responsibility for killing the Highways Bill is upon the Senate, and whether in a future Highways Bill or otherwise they attempt to invade the prerogative of the Commons of this country the Bill which they so attempt to mutilate will be rejected by this House for such has always been the practice of this House whether under Liberal or Conservative Government. But the Senate cannot by rejecting the Bill in this roundabout method get rid of the responsibility that we fix upon them now, and that will sit upon them for all time to come.

Mr. Speaker, my first remarks will be directed to you: I say I am

satisfied and happy to see you back in good health ready to take up once more the labours of the session. I beg of you to accept my heartiest New Year's greetings for yourself and family.
I listened with pleasure to the hon. Solicitor General (Mr. Meighen), who has just taken his seat. As usual he has shown ability. He is a good lawyer, with a great deal of experience, but at the same time' a hair splitter. He was well deserving of promotion.
I have not forgotten that during the session of last year, he succeeded in putting through the House a closure rule. He satisfied his friends that the members of the Opposition should be gagged, and thus attained his object. He was paid spot cash. He is now entrusted with the position of Solicitor General. He is doing well, let him keep on.
To-night he spoke for almost an hour and a half in an endeavour to make us believe that the Dominion Parliament has jurisdiction over our public highways. That is quite a feat. That is a money bill, he says. No, it is not a money bill, but it is a silver bill we passed. Those Senators are ignorant people. The leader of the majority in the Senate, Sir George Ross, who has spent his life in various legislative assemblies and was for a long time the prime minister of his province, does not know anything. The hon. member for Portage-la-Prairie (Mr. Meighen) is the only one who knows anything. He is the learned one. No one else is acquainted with the constitutional law of this country; as regards any others, it is absurd, farcical, a proof of ignorance to say so. You know nothing, he says, and I know all.
What a killer, what a smotherer of the members of the loyal Opposition. He got what he was after, a post of honour, and he chuckles over it. He used to brand us as patronage seekers; now he has slipped into our boots; he is there and we are here.
The hon. member for Red-Deer (Mr. Clark) is also an ignoramus. There are here grey-haired men who have spent their lives in this Parliament, but they are not any the wiser on that account. They are deaf, blind, ignorant, without any acquaintance with the laws of the country. I alone am acquainted with them, I am the only professor, a second Napoleon forsooth.
If we are to believe the hon. Solicitor General, the Dominion Parliament has the right to do anything it pleases. Now, who
.
will believe it? According to his contention, the Dominion Parliament has control over the highways. Now that is rather startling.
The Solicitor General has set himself to the task of teaching a lesson to everybody. However, we also have studied the law oi the land, we grasped its purport before he did, before he became a professor. And we know perfectly well that the Dominion Parliament exercises those powers only which have been conceded by the various provinces of Canada. It does not possess any other than those which were delegated to it. The Dominion Parliament has no control whatever over highways. According to the Solicitor General they would be under that Parliament's control, while at the same time it could not be compelled to say how much money was going to be spent on those highways, in what districts they were to be built, or under whose supervision. No one has any information as to that.
But the hon. Solicitor General finally sought salvation in the direct agency argument. We have heard of that before. The Senate who are better posted than you in respect to the constitution, have decided that there is no direct agency governing this country.
Mr. Chairman, it is getting late, and in accordance with arrangements made, I understand, I shall now move the adjournment of the debate, in case there should actually be, as I believe an agreement to that effect.
